query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A two‐step severe deformation process—comprising cryo‐rolling followed by a brief warm rolling anneal at 600–700 °C—will refine the lamellar architecture in eutectic high-entropy alloys and create localized residual compressive stresses at colony boundaries, thereby hindering microcrack initiation and propagation, and simultaneously enhancing both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the as‐cast lamellar colony baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Two-step severe deformation process: initial cryo-rolling followed by moderate-temperature warm rolling (600–700 °C for short anneals).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; processing parameters must ensure critical microstructural changes during cryo-rolling and controlled partial recrystallization during warm rolling.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-gradient microstructure characterized by refined B2 and L12 (or equivalent) lamellae with localized areas of partial recrystallization and induced residual compressive stresses at colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Cryo-rolling introduces high dislocation densities and stored strain energy, while the subsequent warm rolling promotes partial dynamic recovery and localized recrystallization. These processes reduce stress concentrations at internal boundaries and inhibit microcrack nucleation and propagation, thereby allowing improved plastic accommodation during tensile deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant improvement in both tensile strength (yield and ultimate) and ductility relative to the unmodified, as-cast condition, with reduced microcrack formation observed at lamellar boundaries.
generation.baseline: As-cast dual-phase lamellar colonies of the eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting limited ductility and brittle failure due to microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only when the sequential processing (cryo-rolling immediately followed by a controlled warm rolling anneal in the narrow temperature window of 600–700 °C) is applied; deviations in temperature, annealing duration, or processing sequence may not yield the desired dual-gradient microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement remains uncertain and may depend on precise process control and the specific alloy composition. There is also uncertainty regarding the uniformity of the induced residual compressive stresses across all colony boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a series of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples using the proposed two-step severe deformation intervention (cryo-rolling followed by warm rolling at 600–700 °C for a short duration) and compare their room-temperature tensile properties and microstructural characteristics to a control group of as-cast samples. Detailed microstructural analysis (e.g., EBSD and TEM) should be conducted to examine grain size, recrystallized regions, and residual stress distribution at colony boundaries.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength via standard tensile tests
Microscopic analysis (EBSD, TEM) to assess the presence of dual-gradient architecture and recrystallized zones
Residual stress mapping at lamellar colony boundaries (e.g., using X-ray diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural analyses reveal no reduction in microcrack-prone boundary features (i.e., no formation of localized residual compressive stresses or dual-gradient structure), the hypothesis will be falsified.

These researchers claimed that the above temperature range can be divided into three regions, each one characterized by different deformation behavior. According to Senkov et al. [], at temperatures up to 600 °C twinning compensates for restricted dislocation mobility. At 800 °C Grain Boundary Sliding (GBS) is not yet supported by sufficient dislocation mobility and diffusion leads to cavitation at grain boundaries, while at 1000–1200 °C cavitation at grain boundaries disappears and Dynamic Recrystallization (DRX) occurs. DRX processes are assumed to be responsible for the rapid drop in the flow stress after yielding followed by a steady state flow. Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. A higher annealing temperature allows for a sample to complete its recrystallization earlier, and it also coarsens recrystallized grains at a faster rate. A greater accumulation of strain energy also provides more driving force for enhancing the nucleation and grain growth rate of recrystallization. decision.trend: Early work introduced eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) with alternating soft/hard phases, achieving promising strength–ductility combinations but facing room-temperature brittleness. Subsequent efforts employed thermomechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling, friction stir and warm rolling) to refine and reorganize lamellae, generating hierarchical microstructures that temporarily enhanced ductility. Some studies reversed matrix/precipitate morphologies (e.g., BCC + B2) to improve plasticity of otherwise brittle phases. Despite these advances, controlling microcrack initiation at lamellar boundaries has remained challenging, and fully mitigating room-temperature brittleness without sacrificing strength has proven elusive.
decision.unsolved: While hierarchical or inverted microstructures improve strength–ductility synergy, fundamental microcrack nucleation and coalescence at lamellar boundaries have not been eliminated. Persistent boundary stress concentrations and lamellar mismatch still trigger room-temperature fracture before significant plasticity can accumulate. A single, scalable intervention that robustly suppresses boundary-assisted crack propagation remains unproven in EHEAs.
decision.lever: Adopt a two-step severe deformation process via cryo-rolling followed by moderate-temperature warm rolling (e.g., 600–700 °C for short anneals) to produce a dual-gradient architecture that refines the B2 and L12 lamellae, introduces residual compressive stresses at colony boundaries, and creates a partial recrystallization gradient to impede microcrack propagation at room temperature.
decision.why: Based on evidence from friction stir processing, cryo-rolling, and hierarchical lamella engineering in EHEAs (PMC5818523, PMC6353877, PMC6687781) and the utility of matrix/precipitate inversion (PMC5995863), this multi-step thermomechanical route can hinder boundary cracking, preserving high strength while improving ductility. The testable hypothesis is that partial dynamic recovery and localized recrystallization at lamellar boundaries will reduce crack-driving stresses and enhance plastic accommodation. If tensile tests at room temperature reveal no improvement in fracture strain compared to as-cast lamellar colonies—and if boundary cracks still dominate fracture—then the hypothesis is falsified, indicating that the proposed gradient architecture is insufficient or that other boundary-engineering strategies are required.
